Zhytomyr New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zhytomyrska oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Zhytomyr's Jewish community grew despite an official ban on settlement — 346 Jews were recorded in 1751 regardless — and endured a 1753 blood libel trial that saw 13 of 33 accused Jews executed. The town became a major Hasidic center and, from the mid-19th century, hosted one of only two Jewish printing presses permitted anywhere in the Russian Empire (the other was in Vilnius); by 1897 the community numbered 30,748 (46.6 percent of the population), supporting 27 synagogues and extensive educational and welfare institutions. Zhytomyr's Jews founded 13 agricultural colonies in the Kherson District — likely including some of the farm colonies separately documented elsewhere in this collection — and a Chabad yeshiva operated underground here from 1934 to 1937. Most of the community was murdered during the German occupation between July and October 1941, though some escaped to join the partisans; a small community survives in Zhytomyr today. This cemetery, likely founded in the 19th century, also served the Jewish communities of Korostyshiv, Levkiv, and Stara Kotel'nia, and — notably — hundreds of non-Jewish victims of Stalin's purges were also buried here in the 1930s.
